Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.

Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.

Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

But doctors stress it is a long way from knowing how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.

Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.

The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.

"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.

Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.

Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.

The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.

Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.

tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients

just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear

for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans

Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include , external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

MN202611_1s8jxmqcu3k.t:
Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature

A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pentest Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely, or in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11th and 12th October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On the 1st and 2nd of November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

Each RDM controller can be used to remotely control the temperature of dozens of fridges and freezers

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included, dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there is no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continues to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

Hospital doctors also took strike action in June 2026

Resident doctors are set to return to the picket lines on Friday in a strike over pay.

They will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 GMT, marking their second such action this year .

British Medical Association (BMA) members voted in favour of industrial action after the union rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise from an independent pay body.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he remained committed to delivering the pay award and that he would "do everything in my power" to implement it this year - but said he was unable to do so in the absence of a Stormont budget .

Dr Steven Montgomery, the chairman of the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said doctors should not have to strike for a second time but the issues that had originally taken them to the picket lines remained unresolved.

"Our pay is eroding and we need to address that in order to retain young doctors in Northern Ireland," he said.

Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues

Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay

Healthcare workers at 'tipping point' as union ballots for industrial action

Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor.

Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 GMT on Monday.

They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place.

SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts.

The three branches of hospital doctors also took strike action in June .

During this period of strike action more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled across the health and social care system, according to the health minister.

Steven Montgomery says doctors face burnout due to pressure on them at work

Butler said the fresh action planned for Friday and Monday would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery", especially during the busy winter period.

In England, consultant doctors have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government.

Montgomery said colleagues wanted the best for the health service and their patients but were facing burnout and emotional distress due to work pressure, with their pay failing to reflect the demands placed upon them.

He said doctors wanted full "pay restoration", adding that the annual pay rise they were due to receive would not make up for the value their pay had lost over many years.

Montgomery added that the BMA was "more than willing" to discuss with the minister and Department of Health how pay "erosion" could be addressed and what steps were needed to reassure members that there was a commitment to resolving it.

The BMA balloted its members over a four-week period

Butler said the recommended 3.5% rise was higher than that for other healthcare professionals working in Northern Ireland's health system.

He added that to go beyond the recommended offer would lead to "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

"It comes on top of an average cumulative pay uplifts over the last three years of 30% for resident doctors, 25% for speciality, associate specialist, and specialist doctors, and 24% for consultants," he said.

The minister said he had met the BMA and outlined the financial constraints facing the Department of Health and his intention to issue the pay rises as soon as possible.

But he said that would require adequate funding to be given to his department.

MN202611_17qexxb7ue5.t:
Northern Uganda is suffering from a severe drought

In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.

A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.

"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.

"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."

Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.

Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.

In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.

Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.

"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.

He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.

"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.

After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.

"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."

A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.

"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.

The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.

The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.

But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.

He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.

Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.

'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted

Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.

Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.

Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.

But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.

"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."

Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.

"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.

She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation

African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."

The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.

Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.

But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.

"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.

Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

The walls of the sand dams store water underground when the rivers dry up

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.

But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.

Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.

"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.

"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

MN202611_gpfmhg8iya.t:
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

Airbnb host Lisa Clewes said her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.

The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.

Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.

Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".

He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

Casey and Manny often eat at their desk and their favourite pretzel snack is causing some problems given how sticky and crumbly it is

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher says it's important all of her employees are mindful about the food they are eating at their desk

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Finance worker Laura takes a lunch and dinner break when she's working long hours

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

Marwa was pregnant and new to the UK when her father died in Egypt

We're all going to die - and whether we think about it consciously or not, we generally hope that it will be as smooth as possible for ourselves and our loved ones.

But a study published earlier this year by King's College London and the University of Sheffield suggests that your ethnicity could play a role in how likely this is to be the case.

The research found that people from minority ethnic backgrounds experiencing end-of-life care and grief often struggled to access culturally and religiously appropriate support.

One woman told researchers a hospital sent an Imam - a Muslim religious leader - to her father's bedside when he was dying, even though their family were Hindu.

That lack of culturally appropriate resources or training is exacerbating an "incredibly difficult time in their lives where they were really vulnerable", says Sabrina Bajwah, one of the study's co-authors.

So how can our ethnic or cultural background shape what kind of death we have? And what kind of support is available?

Bajwah told the BBC researchers discovered different types of inequality in their research.

"There was the structural racism that people talked about, which was the 'treating everybody equally' - and by treating everybody equally, services weren't meeting the needs of these communities," she said. "Then there was the other, direct form of racism."

A study last year from the NHS Race and Health Observatory, set up in 2021 to try and tackle racial inequalities within the wider healthcare system, found there was an "alarming" lack of trust among some ethnic minority groups in the care or service they receive.

For example, just over half of participants said they had experienced some form of discrimination from their healthcare providers.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care, which commissioned this year's study, told the BBC that "ethnicity or background should never be a barrier to accessing bereavement support and everyone has the right to the same level of care".

"We will consider the findings of this research project carefully as part of future policy making," they said.

Pravin and his wife of 41 years, Gita, who he describes as a "strong, determined woman"

Pravin Navekar's wife Gita started experiencing chronic pain in her back and legs in 2010, but despite multiple GP visits over a two-year period, was repeatedly sent home with pain relief and no further investigations.

In the end the couple, from Leicester, paid to see a consultant privately, at which point Gita was referred for a CT scan. This picked up a rare cancer, a synovial sarcoma, in her pelvis.

Though she was given a prognosis of under five years when she was first diagnosed, Gita lived for another 11, before passing away in April 2021.

Pravin felt culturally appropriate care was "lacking" at times when Gita was in hospital.

"We're all individuals and we have individual needs and wants, and they're tied in with your faith, your culture, your beliefs," he said.

"If she was in hospital for Diwali, then it was another normal day. But when you have Christmas they do all sorts of things and make people really comfortable… [for Diwali] they don't even acknowledge it. There's nothing wrong with a nurse or a doctor coming up to you and saying, 'Good morning, and happy Diwali to you'.

"It's about recognising a person as a whole person, rather than somebody in a bed who needs care."

Gita pictured at the couple's house in India, which they had hoped to retire to before her diagnosis

When Marwa Soliman's father died in 2013, she had just moved from Egypt to Nottingham and was pregnant with her third child. She didn't know anyone, and had struggled to find a community.

"I just remember crumbling on the floor and crying, not knowing what to do and feeling alone and afraid," she said.

Community group Heya started with just 50 women, but now has more than 700

Six years later, Marwa set up a support group for Muslim, Arabic-speaking women called Heya - meaning "she" in Arabic.

It's grown from 50 women at the start to more than 700. If there's a death in the community, they all rally around to support each other.

"People send condolences and speak to each other, read the Quran together, we can send out timings if they'd like people to visit," she said.

Marwa has since lost three other close family members, including her mother - but she says having Heya made the experience completely different.

"When the other deaths happened, I had hot food, people coming over, people calling… It's a beautiful thing," she said.

But she worries that other communities won't have the same support, and that funding is scarce for the groups that do exist.

"I think there should be more research, and a clear support and referral path with information about where to go and who to speak to," she said.

Marwa's mother, seated on the right, came to visit her and the Heya community group

Marwa's experience, and the group she set up because of it, could be an example to the Department of Health and Social Care, Catriona Mayland, one of the study's co-authors from Sheffield University, told the BBC.

"Services shouldn't look to replace what's already there," she said. "There's some real strengths within communities that we've seen, and [we should think] actually, how can we build on that and work together?"

GTA 6 central characters Lucia and Jason

Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment release in history following the blockbuster video game's launch on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure has sold more than 24.5 million units as of Thursday, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

GTA 6 is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest game follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.

GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.

The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play the game.

Mu itangazo Minisiteri y’Uburezi yashyize ahagaragara kuri uyu wa 19 Ugushyingo 2026, yavuze ko iperereza ryakorewe abakandida 1.097 bari babanje gukekwaho gukopera.

Muri bo, 30 basanze nta buriganya bakoze, bityo amanota yabo aratangazwa. Ku rundi ruhande ariko iperereza ryagaragaje ko hari abandi bakandida 563 bakopeye, bituma umubare w’abanyeshuri bose byemejwe ko bakopeye ugera ku 1.630.

Aba banyeshuri 563, Minisiteri y'Uburezi yavuze ko amanota n'impamyabumenyi byabo byateshejwe agaciro ndetse ko Ikigo Gishinzwe Ibizamini n’Ubugenzuzi bw’Amashuri (NESA) kizamenyesha buri mukandida ibyemezo by’iperereza bitarenze kuri uyu wa Gatanu tariki 20 Ugushyingo 2026.

Minisiteri kandi yasobanuye kandi ko iperereza ku kibazo cyo gukopera ryarangiye burundu, kandi ko nta bindi bizakomeza gukorwaho iperereza.

Ku banyeshuri basanze barakopeye, Minisiteri y’Uburezi yabahaye amahirwe yo gukomeza amasomo yabo, ariko bagomba kubikora binyuze muri bumwe mu buryo bubiri.

Uburyo bwa mbere ni ugusubira mu mwaka wa nyuma w’amashuri yisumbuye ku ishuri basanzwe bigaho cyangwa bakimukira ku rindi, hubahirijwe amabwiriza agenga iyakirwa ry’abanyeshuri.

Imihanda ya Goma irasukurwa, amakamyo atwara imyanda akunze kugaragara mu mihanda, amatara yo ku mihanda yongeye gukora. Ubu hateganywa n'indi mishinga minini y'iterambere.

Umushinga mushya wo kubaka inzu zisaga 3,000 urateganywa mu nkengero z'umujyi wa Goma, mu burasirazuba bwa Repubulika Iharanira Demokarasi ya Congo (RDC), mu gihe ikibazo cy'imiturire gikomeje gukomera muri uyu mujyi munini kurusha indi mu karere.

Uyu mushinga witwa Ngabo City, utegurwa n'ikigo cy'ubwubatsi cyo muri Congo cyitwa JM Construction. Biteganyijwe ko aya mazu azubakwa mu gace ka Nzulo, muri Teritwari ya Masisi, mu Ntara ya Kivu y'Amajyaruguru, ku birometero 15 uvuye mu mujyi wa Goma.

Uyu mushinga uzakorerwa ku buso bugera kuri hegitari 160. Uretse inzu zo guturamo, uzaba urimo amashuri, ikigo nderabuzima n'inzu z'ubucuruzi.

Ni umwe mu mishinga ikomeye y'iterambere y'ubuyobozi bwa FRN mu burasirazuba bwa Congo. Wamurikiwe abayobozi b'intara ku wa 18 Ugushyingo, mu nzu ndangamurage ya Musée de Himbi, mu mujyi wa Goma.

Wakiriwe neza na Guverineri w'Intara ya Kivu y'Amajyaruguru, Bahati Musanga Erasto, wari uhagarariwe na Visi Guverineri ushinzwe Iterambere, Chadrack Amani Bahati.

Uyu guverineri yashyizweho na Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), iyobowe n'umutwe wa March 23 Movement (M23), nyuma y'uko ihuriro ry'iyo mitwe rifashe umujyi wa Goma ku wa 27 Mutarama 2025, rikawugira icyicaro cy'ubuyobozi bw'intara.

Muri icyo gikorwa kandi hari abayobozi bashinzwe ibijyanye n'ubwubatsi n'ibindi bikorwa remezo, abagize ubuyobozi bw'intara, abayobozi b'inzego z'ibanze ndetse n'abayobozi gakondo.

Ibiganiro byibanze ku bijyanye n'imiterere ya tekiniki y'umushinga, uko uzashyirwa mu bikorwa n'ingamba z'umutekano zizawuherekeza.

Umuyobozi Mukuru wa JM Construction, Pierre Gatama, yavuze ko imirimo yo kubaka izatangira vuba. Icyakora, nta ngengabihe irambuye y'uko imirimo izakorwa, ibiciro by'inzu cyangwa uburyo bwo kuzishyura bwatangajwe.

Izo nzu zigenewe abantu bazifuza kuzibamo, bakiyandikisha kugira ngo bazigireho uburenganzira bwo kuzibona. Uyu mushinga ntiwatangajwe nk'igikorwa cyo kubaka inzu za Leta zishyurirwa n'ingengo y'imari ya Leta.

Goma ihanganye n'ikibazo gikomeye cy'imiturire

Goma ni umwe mu mijyi minini kandi ihora irimo ibikorwa byinshi mu burasirazuba bwa Congo. Uherereye ku nkengero z'Ikiyaga cya Kivu, ahateganye n'Akarere ka Rubavu mu Rwanda.

Nubwo nta barura rusange ry'abaturage riherutse gukorwa ku mugaragaro, imibare y'igereranya igaragaza ko uwo mujyi utuwe n'abaturage bagera kuri miliyoni ebyiri.

Goma kandi ni ihuriro rikomeye ry'ubucuruzi n'ubwikorezi. Kuba yegereye uduce dukungahaye ku mabuye y'agaciro, ubucuruzi bwambukiranya imipaka ndetse n'ubwikorezi bw'ibicuruzwa, byawuhaye agaciro gakomeye mu bukungu bw'akarere.

Icyakora, inyungu zituruka muri ibyo bikorwa ntizigera ku baturage bose ku rugero rumwe. Abenshi baracyahanganye n'ubukene n'imibereho mibi.

Imyaka myinshi y'amakimbirane mu bice by'icyaro byo mu Ntara ya Kivu y'Amajyaruguru na yo yatumye abantu benshi bimukira mu mujyi wa Goma no mu nkengero zawo.

Uyu mujyi wakiriye kenshi imiryango y'abavuye mu byabo ishaka aho kuba mu mutekano, bikarushaho kongera igitutu ku miturire yari isanzwe idashamaje ndetse no kuri serivisi rusange.

Imiryango itandukanye itanga ubutabazi yagaragaje ko abantu benshi mu nkengero za Goma batuye mu nzu z'agateganyo z'abavanywe mu byabo zubatswe mu buryo buciriritse.

Ku miryango myinshi, kubona inzu iboneye kandi ihendutse biracyari ikibazo gikomeye. Hari abatuye mu duce twuzuyemo abantu benshi, mu gihe abandi baba mu nzu z'agateganyo zidafite serivisi z'ibanze zihagije.

Umushinga wa Ngabo City uri gutangazwa nk'imwe mu ngamba zo guhangana n'ibyo bibazo. Kuba uzubakwa hanze ya Goma bishobora no gutuma umujyi waguka, aho gukomeza kwagukira mu duce dusanzwe dutuwe cyane.

Mu mezi ashize, ubuyobozi bw'Intara ya Kivu y'Amajyaruguru bwagiye bushimangira gahunda zo guteza imbere ibikorwa remezo, birimo imihanda, ibigo nderabuzima n'amashuri. Uyu mushinga w'imiturire wongeyeho ikindi cyerekezo muri izo gahunda.

Icyakora, haracyari kurebwa niba Ngabo City izagera ku ntego zayo. Iby'ingenzi bigomba kubanza gusobanuka harimo ba nyir'ubutaka buzubakwaho, isuzuma ry'ingaruka ku bidukikije no ku mibereho y'abaturage, ibiciro by'inzu ndetse n'ibikorwa remezo bizakenerwa kugira ngo ibihumbi by'abaturage bizaba muri uwo mudugudu bishobore kubona serivisi zikenewe.

Kugeza ubu, Ngabo City iracyari umushinga munini w'iterambere uteganyijwe, aho kuba umushinga w'imiturire wamaze kubakwa cyangwa kubona inkunga yose izawushyira mu bikorwa.

Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left

An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".

"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts

The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.

Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.

Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.

Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.

Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.

Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.

"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.

On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"

According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."

Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,

Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.

Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.

A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."

The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.

Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.

The bill has been proposed by Nigeria's president

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.

The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.

It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.

Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.

The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.

It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.

Ekpenyong has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.

He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.

"Anyone attempting suicide will ensure that the attempt is successful in order to avoid criminal charges, if he or she survives," he said.

He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.

Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.

"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, you better succeed. If you don't succeed, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.

However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.

"I did not include people who are mentally disturbed because they don't have a mental balance to know what they are doing," he said.

He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.

Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.

"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.

Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.

Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.

Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.

Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.

Ihuriro ry'ibigo riyobowe n'Abanyamerika, rizwi nka Frontier Minerals, ryatsindiye isoko ryo guteza imbere umushinga wo gucukura amabuye y'agaciro mu gace ka Mrima Hill muri Kenya, ritsinda abandi bahataniraga isoko barindwi, barimo ibigo byo mu Bushinwa no muri Australia.

Bivugwa ko aho hantu hari amabuye y'agaciro y'ingenzi afite agaciro karenga miliyari 60 z'amadolari ya Amerika.

Muri ayo mabuye harimo Niobium, ikoreshwa mu gukora ibinyabiziga bikoresha amashanyarazi, igakoreshwa mu ikoranabuhanga ry'indege no mu ikoranabuhanga rya gisirikare.

Frontier Minerals yatangaje ko umushinga wayo ugamije gutuma inyungu nyinshi zituruka kuri ayo mabuye zisigara muri Kenya binyuze mu gutunganya no gusukura ayo mabuye, bikorewe imbere mu gihugu.

Aya masezerano aje mu gihe Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika zirimo gushaka uburyo bwo kubona amabuye y'agaciro menshi yo muri Afurika, hagamijwe gukomeza urwego rw'ibikorwa byo kubona no gutunganya ibikoresho by'ibanze bikenerwa n'inganda zo muri Amerika ndetse no guhangana n'u Bushinwa.

Frontier Minerals igizwe n'ibigo bitatu byo muri Amerika ari byo Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation na ReElement Technologies Corporation.

Iri huriro rihuza ubunararibonye mu guteza imbere ubucukuzi bw'amabuye y'agaciro, mu gutanga ibikoresho by'ingenzi bikenerwa mu nganda no mu ikoranabuhanga rigezweho rikoreshwa mu kuyatunganya.

Kimwe mu bice by'ingenzi bigize umushinga wabo ni ugushyiraho ubushobozi bwo gutunganyiriza no kongerera agaciro amabuye y'agaciro muri Kenya.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Brad Barnett, uhagarariye Frontier Minerals, yavuze ko icyo kigo cyifuza ko Kenya yungukira byinshi ku mutungo kamere wayo.

Agace ka Mrima Hill gaherereye mu Ntara ya Kwale, hafi y'inkengero z'inyanja y'u Buhinde muri Kenya.

Ako gace gafite ubuso bungana na hegitari zigera 158 z'ishyamba.

Icyakora, gahunda yo gucukura amabuye y'agaciro muri ako gace yateje impungenge mu baturage bahatuye.

Bavuga ko batinya ko uwo mushinga ushobora kwangiza iryo shyamba ndetse ukabangamira umurage basigiwe n'abasekuruza babo.

Hari kandi ibibazo byibazwa ku bijyanye n'inyungu zizagera ku baturage batuye hafi y'aho umushinga uzakorera.

Barnett yashimangiye ko Abanyakenya bazabyungukiramo, agira ati: "Turateganya guhanga imirimo irambye ku bakozi bo muri Kenya, bakagira uruhare ku bucuruzi buhakorerwa, bakagira uruhare mu kuzamura ubukungu bw'igihugu no kububyaza umusaruro, binyuze mu kongerera abaturage ubushobozi no gushora imari mu buryo bugamije inyungu rusange, mu gihe tunashyira imbere kurengera ibidukikije no kubahiriza amabwiriza."

Icyakora, iryo huriro riracyasabwa kubona uruhushya rwo gukora ubushakashatsi ku mabuye y'agaciro no kuzuza ibisabwa n'amategeko agenga ubucukuzi bw'amabuye y'agaciro, mbere y'uko umushinga utangira.

Icyemezo cyo gutanga iri soko nticyashimishije bamwe mu bari bahatanye.

Ibiro ntaramakuru Reuters byatangaje ko amasosiyete abiri yari ahanganye na Frontier Minerals ateganya kukijuririra.

Muri byo harimo ikigo cyo muri Australia cyitwa RareX, kivuga ko Frontier Minerals itubahirije igihe ntarengwa cyo gutanga inyandiko zisaba isoko cyari cyaratanzwe mbere.

Guverinoma ya Kenya yo yakomeje gushimangira ko igikorwa cyo gutanga isoko cyakozwe mu mucyo kandi ku buryo buri wese yari afite amahirwe angana yo guhatanira uwo mushinga.

Uyu mushinga uje mu gihe Amerika yihatira gushaka ahandi yakura amabuye y'agaciro y'ingenzi, kugira ngo igabanye kwishingikiriza ku Bushinwa, igihugu gifite uruhare rukomeye mu gutunganya amwe mu mabuye y'agaciro y'ingenzi ku isi.

Washington imaze igihe ishyiraho ubufatanye n'ibihugu bya Afurika bikungahaye ku mabuye y'agaciro, birimo Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo na Zambiya, mu rwego rwo gushimangira imbaraga mu gukora ibikoresho byifashishwa mu nganda z'imodoka zikoresha amashanyarazi, ikoranabuhanga rya gisirikare n'izindi.

Minisiteri y'Ubucukuzi bw'Amabuye y'Agaciro ya Kenya ivuga ko uru rwego ari ingenzi muri gahunda yayo yo guteza imbere ubukungu no kutabushingira gusa ku ishoramari ry'ubukerarugendo, ubuhinzi na serivisi z'imari.

The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards

Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.

The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.

Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.

Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".

The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.

Dinnington Woodland is one of the sites in Yorkshire which will be a focus of the project

The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.

These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.

Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.

"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.

"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."

The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.

Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.

"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.

"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

Tottenham have played 50 Premier League games since Dejan Kulusevski's last top-flight start in May 2025

"I told my mother. I sat with her and I told her: 'Listen, I don't think I can play any more'," says Dejan Kulusevski in a moving interview about his injury nightmare.

It is 18 months since Tottenham and Sweden winger Kulusevski, 26, last started a competitive match.

Spurs have won the Europa League, sacked both Ange Postecoglou and Thomas Frank, "mutually agreed" to part ways with Igor Tudor and appointed Roberto de Zerbi since the former Juventus player last started a first-team game for his club.

A serious knee injury two weeks from the end of the 2024-25 season forced him to miss the whole of the following campaign, as well as the 2026 World Cup.

"You feel like the whole world has forgotten about you," adds Kulusevski in an interview with Tottenham's in-house media , external about the emotional toll of being out for so long.

Thankfully, the player nicknamed 'Deki' has made a full recovery and is closing in on his first Tottenham start since 11 May 2025.

He is not the only footballer to question their career after having their world turned upside down by injury.

In the women's game, Everton club captain Megan Finnigan recently returned from a cruciate ligament injury after 602 days out. , external

"The amount of times the thought of retirement entered my head during rehab was a lot," Finnigan, 28, tells BBC Sport.

Countless hours in the gym away from team-mates, boredom, setbacks and frustration - what is it like for a player at the peak of their game to miss a season because of injury?

'I am a different man now' - Kulusevski on return after 526 days

Kulusevski out for a 'few months' - Postecoglou

Before Crystal Palace visited Tottenham a fortnight from the end of the 2024-25 campaign, Kulusevski had much to look forward to.

Off the pitch, he was making plans to marry his partner Eldina Ahmic, a former midfielder with Swedish club Brommapojkarna and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

On the pitch, there was a Europa League final against Manchester United coming up.

Everything changed in that match against Palace.

In the early stages, Kulusevski stayed down after a challenge with Marc Guehi. He was able to climb to his feet and walk unaided off the pitch and straight down the tunnel.

But in that moment, his problems were only just starting.

Start of a nightmare for Dejan Kulusevski who goes down injured in May 2025 - and does not play again until October 2026

"It was pain, but it didn't hurt that much," Kulusevski says, recalling the patella and cartilage injury in his right knee.

"I could feel that the knee was moving a little bit too much."

The initial diagnosis from Tottenham was that the £25m signing from Juventus, who arrived in the summer of 2023, would be out for "at least a few months".

Due to complications, those months turned into a year and Kulusevski's dream career threatened to turn into a nightmare.

He travelled to Bilbao on crutches to watch his team-mates beat United in the Europa League final.

"That was one of the hardest days of my life," he says. "It was so beautiful to see all the people happy, but for me I was going there with crutches, I couldn't work.

"I couldn't even go and get my medal because it was too slippy to go on that thing [platform].

"Seeing the team celebrating on the bus [outside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] was probably one of the most difficult parts of this journey because you feel so alone.

"You feel like the whole world has forgot about you and what you put in."

As months went by, Kulusevski underwent multiple operations and was even offered a knee transplant as a treatment option, which he rejected.

"You get stressed because nothing works," he says.

Then came another crushing blow delivered in a phone call with Sweden boss Graham Potter. Stockholm-born Kulusevski, who had played for his country since the age of 19, would not be going to the 2026 World Cup.

He had hoped to recover in time to be selected.

"I just stared at the wall for three hours because I really believed I would do it," he says.

It is not just the players who suffer when they are out for so long; the people around them feel the emotional toll as well.

"Seeing him miss the Europa League final and the World Cup, every Premier League game last season, seeing him skipping around on his crutches, those parts were really difficult," Eldina, Kulusevski's wife, says.

'Fantastic moment, fantastic human' - De Zerbi on Kulusevski's long-awaited return

As recently as this past summer, Kulusevski wondered whether he would play again.

"It had been one year and two months and I could still not walk up the stairs like a normal guy.

"I wasn't going to give up, but I also had to think if this didn't work out, what am I going to do, because I am 26 and I have to have some sort of plan."

Enormous comfort came from Leonie, Kulusevski's two-year-old daughter, during his bleakest days.

"I said if I cannot play football any more, I will still have fun with her."

Then, after multiple setbacks, came a crucial breakthrough.

His knee had healed sufficiently for specialists to give him permission to train again.

On 19 October, Kulusevski was given a hero's reception by Spurs fans when he made his first appearance in 526 days.

It came in Tottenham 's 3-1 win over Coventry City as an 87th-minute substitute.

Waiting for him after the final whistle were Eldina and Leonie, his daughter wearing a Spurs shirt with the number 526 on the back, along with the words 'My Hero'.

He made his Sweden return this month, coming off the bench in a win against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

"Every day is just beautiful now," says Kulusevski, who has made four substitute appearances totalling 42 minutes for his club this season.

Research suggests female footballers are two to six times more likely to suffer anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries than their male counterparts.

Everton captain Finnigan remembers how she "completely lost my sparkle" as she endured the long road to recovery.

"It's not comfortable to think back how I was," Finnigan tells BBC Radio Merseyside's Giulia Bould.

"Anyone that knows me knows I'm very bubbly, quite loud, I like to be at the centre of things. I completely lost myself in rehab, completely lost my sparkle as my mum says.

"How I was in this building is not nice to think back on. I was always thinking what other people were thinking about me. I was not pleasant to be around as I was struggling so much.

"I was also thinking 'no-one wants to be around me'. I was just miserable. Everyone in this building has seen me cry over the past 18 months."

Listen: Megan Finnigan 'Really special feeling to be back'

Megan Finnigan, Everton's number 20, returned to competitive action this season after 602 days out following an ACL injury

Finnigan - Everton 's longest-serving women's player having joined the Blues at the age of nine - suffered her injury in an FA Cup tie against Tottenham in January 2025. She did not return to competitive action until September of this year.

"I was in quite a difficult place mentally," she adds.

One thing that helped her through her lowest moments was writing down her feelings.

"It was an absolute whirlwind of a rehab, a rollercoaster," she adds.

"Anyone who went through it with me will tell you that. I am really glad I kept a diary as proof I did it and survived it."

Former Arsenal and England midfielder Fara Williams points to how some players who suffer serious injuries in the Women's Super League face specific worries.

"While they are going through rehab, there are financial worries, bills to pay; they are on short contracts so you don't have that stability," says Williams.

"While you are managing the injury, mentally you are stressing, wondering where the next contract is coming from. When you are stressed, I imagine that doesn't help with the healing of the injury."

Micah Richards suffered multiple long-term knee and hamstring injuries before he retired in 2019 while at Aston Villa .

A few months later the former Manchester City and England defender opened up to BBC Sport about injuries and the "dark side of football".

"I was in a lonely place for a long time, and I did not know how to get out of it," he said at the time.

"Deep down, I probably knew it was already over, but for most of the two and a half years between my 295th and final game as a professional, against Wolves in October 2016, and the day I announced my retirement in July 2019, I was living in denial.

"I could run and I could jump - but I couldn't twist on my right knee, and it would not get any better. Whatever I tried, it did not make any difference.

"There were times while I was injured at Villa when I felt like I was a ghost.

"They told me to come in three times a week, then two. Then one.

"I would go into the gym and tell myself 'I am all right, I am all right, I am all right' but actually I had no idea how to deal with what was happening to me, and my body."
