MN202611_186inqwal5i.t:
Tony Mowbray started his managerial career with Hibernian

The overwhelming support from the world of football for Blackburn Rovers boss Tony Mowbray has come as no surprise to interim head coach Damien Johnson.

Mowbray announced on Wednesday he was stepping back from his role at the Championship club because of health issues with Johnson and Mike Dodds taking charge "for the time being".

The news sparked an outpouring of messages of support from EFL clubs and further afield.

"To someone like me, it's not a surprise," Johnson said.

"I've known him for over 10 years, but I think people who have only known him in this club for the four or five months he's been in, they can see that. That's just the impact Tony has on people, it's just a testament to Tony and his nature and how he is and how he treats people."

Mowbray, 62, returned to Ewood Park in June for a second spell as head coach and has taken them to 13th place in the Championship after they finished just five points clear of the relegation zone last season.

The former Middlesbrough and West Brom boss had previously taken time out of the game during his spell as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.

Boro head coach Kim Hellberg was one of the first to send his best wishes to one of his predecessors.

"He's a brilliant guy. It was really good to meet him and he was absolutely brilliant every time I've talked to him," Hellberg said.

"He's a brilliant football coach. He's done a lot of good things. He's a brilliant human being and you can see everyone knows that."

Rovers have won five of their past nine league games with Johnson crediting Mowbray's impact at the club for creating a more positive atmosphere.

"When the statement came out there was concern - we care a lot about Tony and it was a little bit of a shock - we want what's best for him at this time," Johnson told BBC Radio Lancashire.

"Tony has built a real bond with the whole group and with everyone at the whole club, so there was naturally concern for him and a bit of emotion for a day or so but we all hold him in the highest regard - we hope he's given the privacy he needs.

"He sent a private message to the players which was read out today [Friday] and they appreciated it. He's sent some private messages to staff but Tony's allowed us just to get on, he'll be allowed the time he needs and we'll just get on with the game."

Blackburn visit Burnley on Sunday (12:00 GMT) hoping to end a 10-game winless run against their Lancashire rivals, who have not won a home game in the league since 18 October last year.

Johnson says the match is their main focus rather than what may happen with the managerial situation down the line.

"We've just been focused fully on the game, we know it's a huge game and we've been working with the team throughout the week. The discussions have been about the game and nothing else," he added.

Meanwhile, Blackburn are set to be without goalkeeper Balazs Toth until the new year after he told Hungarian media , external he suffered a hand injury while playing for his national side against Northern Ireland on Tuesday.

"The situation is not that good, but for now it looks like I will be able to avoid surgery," he said before travelling back to England to have the injury assessed by Blackburn.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) with director of football Jason Wilcox

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the Old Trafford club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.

MN202611_cjm5g4i4tu.t:
Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported £316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

"It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis."

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established."

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need."

MN202611_239rl16q0z.t:
Carys Douglas said her Oscar-winning parents taught her that "building my own identity depended on me and no one else"

Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.

Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific" . It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and that she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.

Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Catherine Zeta Jones has declared the phrase "nepo baby" is "horrific"

Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.

She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.

The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.

Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".

"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.

Carys Douglas described Three Cliffs Bay in Gower Peninsula, Swansea, as "stunning"

Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.

Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.

"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.

"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.

She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".

"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The governments own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own assessment.

This deal will matter for food exporters, and certain types of energy producer. It may not have a clearly visible impact at the checkout.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

MN202611_1wx9wz22tfw.t:
Reinaldo Dennes was convicted over the murder of a diamond dealer in 1996

A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

How widely used is the death penalty in the US?

The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murderer, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.

Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major AI data centre project in Canada that has so far been embraced by legislators.

As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.

While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.

"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.

At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".

One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.

His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.

Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign. , external The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75% , external , from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.

Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.

The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.

The project is billed as "off-grid" , external , relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment , external , arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.

The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June , external that he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".

In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.

Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.

"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.

Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.

He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.

Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.

"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press , external , held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.

This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.

There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.

On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre , external that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.

But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.

"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.

"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.

BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the US

So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.

The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.

Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.

Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.

"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.

Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.

If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.

MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta, , external over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.

But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.

"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."

Kigali igiye kwakira ku nshuro ya gatatu irushanwa ry’umukino w’iteramakofe rizwi nka Kigali Fight Night, riteganyijwe ku wa 10 Ukuboza 2026 muri BK Arena, aho ryitezwe kuzitabirwa n’abasaga 4.000.

Iri rushanwa ritegurwa na Silverback Sports, rikaba ryaragutse riva ku kuba urwego rwo guhuza abakinnyi b’iteramakofe bakina nk'ababigize umwuga mu Rwanda gusa rikaba rigamije guhinduka urubuga ruhuza abakinnyi bo muri Afurika yose.

Kigali Fight Night izaba muri gahunda y'ibikorwa by’imikino njyarugamba bizwi nka Kigali Fight Weekend, bizamara iminsi 12 aho bizategurwa ku bufatanye na Professional Fighters League (PFL) Africa. Muri ibyo bikorwa hazaba amarushanwa abiri akomeye: Kigali Fight Night yo ku wa 10 Ukuboza na PFL Africa Finals yo ku wa 12 Ukuboza 2026.

Mu mikino iteganyijwe, Jerry Katamba azahura na Mugunge Augustin mu mukino nyamukuru wo guhatanira igikombe. Aba bombi bakomoka i Goma muri Repubulika Iharanira Demokarasi ya Congo.

Mu yindi mikino, Umunyarwanda Aimable H azahura na Chappo Mawe wo muri Tanzania, mu gihe Jean Junior wo muri Cameroun azakina na Mugisha Emma wo mu Rwanda. Hazaba kandi n’indi mikino izahuza abakinnyi baturutse muri Kenya, Gabon, Nigeria no mu bindi bihugu bya Afurika.

Umuyobozi Mukuru wa Silverback Sports, Bashir Ntwari, yavuze ko intego ya Kigali Fight Night atari ugutegura imikino gusa, ahubwo ari ukubaka urubuga ruzafasha abakinnyi b’Abanyafurika kubona amahirwe yo guhatana ku rwego rwo hejuru, kumenyekana no guteza imbere umwuga wabo.

Yagize ati: “Intumbero yacu mu gutegura Kigali Fight Night yamye irenze gutegura imikino y’iteramakofe gusa. Twifuza kubaka urubuga ruzafasha abakinnyi b’Abanyafurika guhatana ku rwego rwo hejuru, kumenyekana no guhabwa agaciro bakwiye, ndetse no kubaka umwuga uhamye muri uyu mukino."

Yavuze kandi ko kuba ku nshuro ya gatatu iri rushanwa rizabera muri BK Arena ni intambwe ikomeye mu kugera kuri iyo ntego. Yashimangiye ko kuba PFL Africa ifitanye ubufatanye na RwandAir buzagira uruhare mu gukurura abafana baturutse mu bihugu bitandukanye no kurushaho guteza imbere imikino njyarugamba muri Afurika.

Mu bufatanye bushya RwandAir ni umufatanyabikorwa w’ingendo zo mu kirere muri Kigali Fight Night aho abifuza kuza i Kigali kwitabira iri rushanwa bazahabwa igabanyirizwa rya 20% ku ngendo z’indege, bakoresheje kode KFN20.

Jermaine Burke, washinze Universal Sports ikorera i Dubai akaba n’Umuyobozi ushinzwe ubucuruzi muri Silverback Sports, yavuze ko Afurika y’Iburasirazuba ifite ubushobozi bwo kuzatanga abakinnyi bakomeye mu iteramakofe, ariko ko hakenewe kubaha amahirwe yo kwitoza no guhatana kenshi aho bishoboka.

Yakomeje agira ati: “Ariko guteza imbere umukino w’iteramakofe ntibigarukira gusa ku gutegura amarushanwa. Ahubwo ni ugushyiraho uburyo bufasha urubyiruko kuvumbura impano zarwo, kubona amahugurwa yo ku rwego rw’umwuga, guhatana kenshi no kubaka umwuga uhamye muri siporo."

Yavuze ko binyuze muri Kigali Fight Night, "twifuza kugira uruhare mu kubaka urwego rwa siporo rukomeye kurushaho, ruha abakinnyi bakiri bato bo muri Afurika amahirwe yo kumenyekana, kubona ubufasha n’ubundi buryo bubafasha kugera ku ntsinzi, haba mu bihugu byabo ndetse no ku rwego mpuzamahanga.”

Kigali Fight Night yatangiye guhuza abakinnyi baturutse mu bihugu 10 bya Afurika, aho mu byiciro byayo bibiri byabanje habaye imikino 16 y’iteramakofe yakinwaga kinyamwuga mu gihe abategura iri rushanwa bafite intego yo kurigira urubuga rukomeye ku mugabane wa Afurika, ruhuza abakinnyi, abashoramari, abategura amarushanwa, ibitangazamakuru n’abafana b'imikino njyarugamba.

Biteganyijwe kandi ko iri rushanwa rizarushaho kumenyekanisha Kigali nk’Umujyi wakira amarushanwa akomeye ya siporo, rikanatanga amahirwe mashya mu rwego rw'ubukerarugendo bushingiye kuri Siporo no mu ishoramari.

Siya Kolisi (right) spoke passionately about what rugby means to South African people in his pre-match news conference

Already circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent days.

Not for the first time, Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus landed himself in hot water with the powers-that-be for criticising match officials.

After receiving a six-match ban for questioning the integrity of referee Andrea Piardi and television match official Matteo Liperini in South Africa's defeat by France last week, Erasmus has been defended and condemned .

There is no doubt, however, over where the Springbok camp stand, with assistant coach Mzwandile Stick throwing his support behind Erasmus.

"He's been hands-on with our team [in the build-up], and we're in a good space," Stick said on Friday.

"Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no-one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure."

Erasmus also said South Africa let their country down in the France game, with captain Siya Kolisi bristling at a suggestion that it was a "dramatic" assessment.

"It might sound dramatic to you, but to us it means so much more," Kolisi said during his pre-match news conference.

"Rugby has done a lot for our country, and it's done a lot for many of us who come from South Africa.

"We know how happy people are and what the mood is like when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it.

"When we play, we think about the people back home. We don't take representing the country lightly because we represent every single person in South Africa when we put on that jersey."

Live on 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

While Erasmus has dominated headlines this week, he will not be in attendance at Aviva Stadium on Saturday.

Instead, in a bizarre twist, the two-time World Cup winner will host a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel, with the conditions of his suspension prohibiting him from matchday contact with players and management.

Whether or not Jasper Wiese joins Erasmus' stream remains to be seen. The back row was hit with a four-match ban for a dangerous ruck clearout against France.

While Wiese's fate did not attract the same level of scrutiny, South Africa's sense of injustice will perhaps be fuelled by the sight of Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast on Saturday.

As predicted by Erasmus , Prendergast was cleared to face the world champions after being cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fiji back row Peceli Yato.

"I will tell you now for free, if that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," said Stick.

"If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle."

Dan Sheehan says he is not fazed by switching to the back of the scrum

Focused on erasing the pain of last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, Ireland have sidestepped questions about Erasmus this week, with head coach Andy Farrell opting not to comment on his opposite number's suspension.

Irish captain Dan Sheehan said the commotion has not "affected the squad at all".

"Obviously it's a big media story for fans to get behind, but in terms of us playing the match it has zero impact," he said.

While there may be added scrutiny on referee Christophe Ridley, Sheehan said he plans to leave the official alone unless compelled to bring something "major" to his attention.

The Irish skipper has enough on his plate anyway. In addition to leading his side against the back-to-back world champions, Sheehan has been thrust into the number eight role.

The 28-year-old has won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker but moves to the back row with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney all ruled out.

Ireland hope Sheehan's inclusion in the back row will facilitate his powerful ball-carrying capabilities, but he insists he is not going to "overthink" it.

"I just get on with stuff. Like, eight on my back, just pick the ball up and go," said Sheehan, whose only previous start in the position was in Leinster's win over Munster last month.

"It can't be that complicated. That's my approach to it, to be honest."

Erasmus will watch Saturday's game from South Africa's team hotel

Had it not been for the furore surrounding Erasmus, chances are the pre-match talk would have been dominated by scrums.

Last year, Ireland were shown five cards and conceded six penalties and a penalty try during a chastening night against the Springbok scrum.

That set-piece shellacking may have given the Irish pack nightmares over the past 12 months, and while South Africa won nine scrum penalties against France, Kolisi expects a closer contest in Dublin this time.

"Their scrum is much better than it was a year ago," he said.

"You can see they're getting penalties. But our focus is not on what they're going to do. It's about making sure we stick to our plans and do what we need to do in the scrum."

The Springboks have been boosted by the return of record cap holder Eben Etzebeth, but his second-row partner Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury on Friday. He has been replaced by Franco Mostert, who was not originally in the matchday squad.

Ireland - who have lost their past six contests against New Zealand, France and South Africa, the three teams above them in the world rankings, by double-digit margins - have also been forced into a late change, with Thomas Clarkson replacing Sam Illo as the replacement tight-head prop.

The myriad permutations mean Ireland and South Africa could meet again in the finals weekend at Twickenham.

Either way, Saturday's sold-out contest in Dublin promises to deliver enough drama to tide fans over until next year's World Cup in Australia, where they could contest the final.

Kinshasa, the capital, has a garbage problem. It doesn’t need billions of dollars to clean. It only requires mobilising the population to keep their neighbours tidy. Yet, government is spending millions of dollars on a ‘bash-Rwanda’ campaign

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is obviously obsessed with Rwanda. It has found yet another target for its complaints among the many projects Rwanda is involved in: a partnership between Kigali and five European countries, Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands, on the resettlement of asylum seekers.

Rather than confronting its own domestic challenges head-on, particularly persistent insecurity, chronic hunger and a deadly Ebola epidemic, Kinshasa has once again chosen to focus on Rwanda’s partnerships.

What the world is witnessing is not the smart diplomacy the Congolese leadership imagines it is practising, but a familiar pattern of complaints, accusations, protests and political grandstanding.

It is difficult to understand how a government that is so utterly failing to address insecurity across its territory, deliver essential public services, contain an epidemic that has now claimed more than 5,000 lives, and meet the basic needs of its population can find so much time and energy to challenge other countries over decisions concerning their own migration and asylum policies.

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are sovereign countries with their own institutions, national interests and foreign policy priorities. They determine their international partnerships through their respective legal and diplomatic frameworks.

Kinshasa’s persistent attempts to sabotage virtually every Rwanda-related international engagement are not just infantile and exhausting; they should raise serious questions about the regime’s priorities and, frankly, the soundness of mind of its leaders.

“Rwanda lives rent-free in Kinshasa’s foreign policy” is the expression that comes to mind. The Tshisekedi regime is obsessed with keeping tabs on Rwanda, opposing its international engagements and mobilising diplomatic pressure against Kigali. Whether it is economic cooperation, tourism, sports diplomacy or development initiatives, Kinshasa seems determined to find something to denounce.

Yet this obsession does nothing meaningful for ordinary Congolese citizens. Condemning Rwanda’s partnership with European countries will not restore security in North Kivu and South Kivu. It will not neutralise armed groups, address the FDLR issue, rebuild public institutions, create jobs or improve the living conditions of millions of Congolese.

The conflicts in eastern DRC require serious political commitment, credible negotiations and concrete action to address the root causes of instability. They cannot be resolved through political theatrics.

More fundamentally, the Tshisekedi regime seems to mistake controversy for leadership. A country’s foreign policy should advance its national interests, strengthen international partnerships, attract investment and contribute to regional stability. It should not become an endless exercise in complaining about what another country is doing.

Kinshasa gives the impression that it has no foreign policy objective besides blocking or denouncing whatever Rwanda proposes or achieves on the international stage. If Kigali secures a partnership, condemn it. If Rwanda launches an initiative, oppose it. If Rwanda receives international recognition, question it.

But where is that same energy when it comes to developing a coherent national vision for the DRC?

The Congolese people deserve leadership that prioritises their well-being. They deserve a government that uses its diplomatic resources to create opportunities for its citizens rather than spending a disproportionate amount of time and energy monitoring its neighbour. A serious state acts, negotiates, builds partnerships and delivers results.

The diplomacy of lamentation achieves nothing in the long run. Rwanda’s partnerships will not disappear simply because Kinshasa disapproves of them. Nor will the DRC resolve its internal challenges by constantly pointing fingers at its neighbour.

The pressing question for Tshisekedi’s administration is not what Rwanda is doing for its people or with its partners. It is what Kinshasa itself is doing for the Congolese people.

KIGALI – Four decades ago, Rwanda and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) began a partnership at a time when access to basic services remained a major challenge for many children and families.

The years that followed would bring profound changes to the country, including the devastation of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and the difficult task of rebuilding families, communities and public institutions.

Throughout this period, UNICEF worked alongside the government to support children through healthcare, immunization, nutrition, education and protection programs. The impact of these efforts is reflected in improvements recorded over the years.

At the celebration of 40 years of UNICEF’s work in Rwanda on Friday, November 20, First Lady Jeannette Kagame said the anniversary was an opportunity to recognize the progress made while renewing the commitment to children who still need support.

Speaking at an event that coincided with World Children’s Day, Mrs Kagame said the partnership should be measured not simply by the number of programs implemented, but by the lives changed through them.

“When I look around this room, I do not just see 40 years of programs, I see 40 years of partnership. Children whose lives were saved through vaccination, those who received protection because someone spoke up for their rights, and others who grew up to become parents, teachers, doctors, leaders and artists because they were supported when they were young,” she said.

Rwanda’s 2025 Demographic and Health Survey found that under-five mortality had fallen from 45 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2020 to 36 in 2025. The same survey recorded a decline in stunting among children under five, from 33 per cent to 27 per cent over the five-year period.

According to the 2025 survey, 94 per cent of children aged 12 to 23 months had received all basic vaccinations, while coverage for measles and three doses of the DPT-containing vaccine stood at 97 per cent.

Education has seen similar expansion. The National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda reported that primary school net enrolment reached 95 per cent in the 2023/24 school year.

These figures help explain Mrs Kagame’s observation that nearly every child now goes to primary school, although access to school does not automatically mean every child completes their education or receives quality learning.

The First Lady said such progress was made possible by the combined efforts of government, UNICEF, civil society, communities, parents and children themselves.

Supporting Girls and Young People To Realize Their Potential

Mrs Kagame also highlighted the partnership between UNICEF and Imbuto Foundation, which has worked for more than two decades to improve opportunities for girls and young people.

The cooperation has supported girls to remain in school, helped adolescent mothers return to education and rebuild their dignity, and promoted early childhood development, youth health, mentorship and efforts to address teenage pregnancy.

She said the two institutions brought complementary strengths to the work. Imbuto Foundation contributed its understanding of Rwandan families and the trust it has built within communities, while UNICEF brought international expertise, resources and evidence.

“Together, we brought change that neither could have achieved alone. The experience shows the value of institutions working together consistently to address the needs of children, rather than treating partnership as simply an agreement between organizations,” she noted.

A Renewed Promise for The Next Generation

Despite the achievements, the First Lady cautioned against treating the anniversary as the end of the work. The latest figures show that 27 per cent of children under five are still affected by stunting, while the need to protect children from violence, neglect and exclusion remains.

She said the next phase of the partnership should ensure that no child is left behind because of where they live, poverty, gender or disability. It should also give children a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lives.

Addressing children at the event and across the country, she reminded them that their importance should not be postponed until they become adults.

“You’re not just the future, you are the present. Your voice matters now, your education matters now, your health matters now, your safety matters now, and your dreams matter now,” she said.

The First Lady highlighted that investing in children is both a moral responsibility and an investment in the country’s future. “When we protect a child, we protect a family. When we educate a child, we transform a nation. And when we believe in a child, we change the future,” she said.

Rebuilding Families and Protecting Vulnerable Children

Minister of Gender and Family Promotion Consolee Uwimana said UNICEF had remained alongside Rwanda through different stages of its development, including the period after the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, when many children were left without parental care and families and communities needed support to rebuild.

She said the partnership contributed to expanding immunization, strengthening maternal and child healthcare, improving nutrition and reducing stunting. It also supported the expansion of early childhood development services, access to education and improvements in water and sanitation.

Rwanda is advancing a national care reform agenda aimed at ensuring that children grow up in safe and loving families rather than institutions. Uwimana highlighted the role of Inshuti z’Umuryango volunteers, who work within communities to help protect children and support families.

She said the Government would continue investing in health, nutrition, education and early childhood development, while strengthening families and supporting parents and caregivers.

“Every Rwandan child must be born safely, grow up in a loving family, have access to quality early learning and education, be protected from violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect,” she said.

UNICEF Regional Director for Eastern and Southern Africa, Etleva Kadilli, joined children and partners in Kigali to mark 40 years of progress for Rwanda’s children, celebrating the gains made while looking ahead to another 40 years of advancing every child’s rights.

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yashimye Ishami ry’Umuryango w’Abibumbye ryita ku Bana (UNICEF) ku bufatanye n’u Rwanda mu myaka 40 ishize, avuga ko muri icyo gihe hari byinshi byagezweho mu kurengera abana, kubaha uburezi, kubitaho no kubafasha kugera ku nzozi zabo.

Yabigarutseho kuri uyu wa Gatanu, tariki ya 20 Ugushyingo 2026, mu birori byo kwizihiza imyaka 40 UNICEF imaze ikorera mu Rwanda, byahuriranye n’Umunsi Mpuzamahanga w’Abana.

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yavuze ko mu myaka 40 ishize, UNICEF yagiranye n’u Rwanda isezerano ry’uko buri mwana, aho yaba yaravukiye hose, umuryango akomokamo cyangwa imimerere arimo, azahabwa amahirwe yo kubaho, gukura neza no kurota ejo hazaza heza.

Ati: “Uyu munsi twateraniye hano kugira ngo twishimire ko iryo sezerano ryubahirijwe.”

Yavuze ko iyo arebye abari bateraniye muri ibyo birori, atabona imyaka 40 y’ibikorwa n’imishinga gusa, ahubwo abona imyaka 40 y’ubufatanye bwatanze umusaruro.

Yatanze urugero rw’abana babashije kubaho kubera ko bakingiwe, abarinzwe kubera ko hari abavuganiye uburenganzira bwabo, ndetse n’abana bakuze bakaba ba ababyeyi, abagabo, abarimu, abaganga, abayobozi n’abahanzi kubera ko hari abababaye hafi bakiri bato bakabafasha gukuza impano zabo.

Yagaragaje ko umusaruro w’imyaka 40 ugaragarira mu buzima bw’abana ku giti cyabo, aho ibikorwa byafashije abana kubarinda icyabahungabanya no kubona amahirwe yo kwiga no kugera ku nzozi zabo.

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yavuze ko amateka y’u Rwanda n'aya UNICEF yagiye akurana, kuva mu bihe by’umwijima mwinshi mu mateka y’igihugu, no mu gihe cyo kongera kubaka igihugu kugeza ku Rwanda ruriho uyu munsi.

Yagaragaje ko muri ibyo bihe, impfu z’abana zagabanutse cyane, abana hafi ya bose bakaba biga mu mashuri abanza, abakobwa bagakomeza amashuri, hakaba hari n’ingamba zo kurwanya igwingira ry’abana kuva ku rwego rw’umudugudu, ndetse abana bakaba batakiri abantu birengagizwa.

Yashimye ubufatanye bwa UNICEF na Imbuto Foundation

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yashimye by’umwihariko ubufatanye bumaze igihe kirekire hagati ya UNICEF na IMbuto Foundation, avuga ko bumaze imyaka isaga 20 bushingiye ku ntego yo kutagira umukobwa n’umwana uwo ari we wese usigara inyuma.

Yavuze ko ibyo bigo byombi byahurije hamwe imbaraga mu gufasha abakobwa gukomeza amashuri, gufasha abangavu babyaye gusubira mu ishuri no kongera kwiyubaka, guteza imbere imikurire myiza y’abana bakiri bato, ubuzima bw’urubyiruko, kuruyobora no kururera, ndetse no kurwanya inda ziterwa abangavu.

Yashimangiye ko ibyo bikorwa bitakozwe hagamijwe kugirira impuhwe urubyiruko, ahubwo byashingiye ku kwemera ubushobozi n’imbaraga zarwo zo kwiteza imbere.

Yasobanuye ko Imbuto Foundation yazanye ubushake n’umutima wo gufasha abantu, igendeye ku kizere abaturage bayifitiye ndetse no gusobanukirwa neza imibereho y’imiryango y’Abanyarwanda, naho UNICEF yo yazanye ubumenyi ifite ku rwego mpuzamahanga, ubushobozi n’ubushakashatsi bifasha kumenya ibisubizo bikwiye.

Avuga ko ibyo byombi byahurije hamwe ubufatanye bikazana impinduka zitari kugerwaho kuri buri ruhande rwonyine.

Ati: “Uko ni ko ubufatanye nyabwo bugaragara. Si ugushyira umukono ku masezerano gusa, ahubwo ni uguhagararana umwaka ku wundi, mu guharanira inyungu z’abana bose.”

Madame Jeannette Kagame yashimiye UNICEF kuba yarizeye ubuyobozi bw’u Rwanda no gukorana na bwo.

Yibukije abana ko ari ingenzi muri iki gihe, atari ejo hazaza gusa

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yavuze ko kwizihiza iyi sabukuru bitagomba kugarukira ku kureba ibyo UNICEF n’u Rwanda bagezeho, ahubwo ko hakenewe no kureba imbere, abantu bakazirikana ko uburenganzira bw’abana atari umushinga warangiye, ahubwo ari isezerano rigomba kubahirizwa buri munsi.

Yabwiye abana bari bitabiriye ibi birori n’abandi bose ko aribo bazaba abayobozi b’ejo hazaza, kandi ko na n’ubu bafite agaciro, ijwi ryabo rikaba rigomba kumvwa kandi ibyifuzo byabo bikitabwaho.

Ati: “Ijwi ryanyu rifite agaciro ubu. Uburezi bwanyu bufite agaciro ubu. Ubuzima bwanyu bufite agaciro ubu. Umutekano wanyu ufite agaciro ubu. N’inzozi zanyu zifite agaciro ubu.”

Yabasabye guharanira gukora neza, bakabaho bafite icyizere, bakagira ubuntu kuri bo ubwabo no ku bandi, ndetse bakemera kugira intego n'inzozi zikomeye zo kugera ku byo bifuza.

Yabijeje ko abakuru batazigera bareka kubizera, ababwira ko abana ari ishema ry’abakuru, bishingiye kubyo bakora n’impano ikomeye bafite.

Yabwiye kandi abantu bakuru bitabiriye ibirori ko inshingano zabo zitararangira, kuko zigomba gukomeza kugeza igihe buri mwana mu Rwanda azashobora kuvuga ko, atekanye, yiga kandi akunzwe.

Madamu Jeannette Kagame yavuze ko mu gihe hizihizwa imyaka 40 ishize UNICEF ikorera mu Rwanda, hakwiye no gushyirwaho irindi sezerano rizagenderwaho mu myaka 40 iri imbere.

Yavuze ko iryo sezerano rikwiye kuba iryo kutagira umwana n’umwe usigara inyuma kubera aho atuye, kuba ari umukobwa, ubukene cyangwa ubumuga afite.

Rikwiye kandi kuba iryo kumva abana no kubatega amatwi aho kubavugisha gusa, ndetse no gushora imari mu bana, atari ukubera ko ari inshingano mbonezamubano gusa, ahubwo ko ari igishoro cyiza igihugu icyo ari cyo cyose gishobora kugira.

Yavuze ko mu myaka 40 ishize UNICEF yaje mu Rwanda kugira ngo ihagararane n’abana, ariko uyu munsi u Rwanda na rwo ruhagaze hamwe na UNICEF kugira ngo ruyishimire.

Yashimiye UNICEF kuba yarakomeje gukorana n’u Rwanda mu myaka 40, kuba yarizeye abana b’Abanyarwanda no mu bihe bitari byoroshye, ndetse no kongera kwibutsa ko ubukomere bw’igihugu butagomba gupimirwa ku nyubako gifite, ahubwo ko bugomba no kureberwa ku buryo gifata abana bakiri bato.

Yagize ati: “Iyo turinze umwana, tuba turinze umuryango. Iyo twigishije umwana, duhindura igihugu. Kandi iyo twizeye umwana, duhindura ejo hazaza.”

Yasoje yifuriza UNICEF Rwanda isabukuru nziza y’imyaka 40, anavuga ko yifuza ko imyaka iri imbere yazatuma buri mwana mu Rwanda arushaho kugira ejo hazaza heza.

Nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India

A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

Nadine Yousif contributed to this report.

Chelsea have been fined £150,000 by the Football Association as part of a punishment for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants during an FA Cup third-round win at Charlton Athletic in January.

The club have also been warned about their future conduct and had an action plan imposed on them in relation to the offence.

"Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief," said an FA statement. , external

Chelsea admitted the charge but had an appeal against the fine issued by an independent regulatory commission rejected.

The FA's written reasons stated that although the discriminatory chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

"We unequivocally condemn this behaviour," said a Chelsea statement. , external "Sectarian abuse - chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group - and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary."

The FA itself was fined by Uefa for a similar incident of chanting, from England's away support during their Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels

Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Crystal Palace forward Ismaila Sarr says he has moved on from Liverpool 's interest in signing him and is keen for a "fresh start" under new manager Thomas Frank.

The Senegal international, 28, is keen to put that episode behind him after Liverpool explored a move at the end of the summer transfer window.

Ultimately, Palace rejected advances for Sarr, who scored 21 goals in 45 games in all competitions last season as his side won the Conference League, while Liverpool opted to keep Cody Gakpo despite interest from Manchester City.

In his first interview since Liverpool 's pursuit of him, Sarr - who has been nominated for the African footballer of the year award - told BBC Sport: " Liverpool is one of the biggest clubs in world football and, when a club like that shows an interest in you, of course it's something you take seriously.

"I don't think any player would be indifferent to that kind of opportunity. It was an interesting possibility, and naturally, I considered what it could mean for my career.

"Today, that chapter is behind me. I've always believed that you can't move forward if you're constantly looking in the rear-view mirror.

"I'm a Crystal Palace player, I'm proud of what we've achieved together, and my focus is on getting back on the pitch and helping the team."

Sarr is still sidelined with a groin injury, but talks are ongoing with Palace over an improved contract - despite his current deal running until 2029.

He added: "Yes, there have been discussions with the club. For now, I prefer to let those conversations happen privately and concentrate on football."

Sarr missed most of Pierre Sage's spell in charge, making just two brief substitute appearances in the Premier League this season.

Sage was replaced by former Tottenham Hotspur and Brentford manager Frank this week.

"Of course, it's a difficult moment for everyone at the club," Sarr said. "After everything we achieved last season, nobody expected us to be in this position.

"But I know the quality of this squad. We have very good players, a strong group and the ability to turn things around.

"The arrival of Thomas Frank is an opportunity for a fresh start, new energy and a different approach. We all have to take responsibility, work together and fight for every point.

"I'm confident we can overcome this difficult period and achieve our objectives this season."

Sarr is on 10-man shortlist for the African Player of the Year award, which will be presented on 7 December in Lagos, Nigeria.

It follows Sarr being named Conference League Player of the Season, scoring nine goals as Palace won their first European title. He also collected both the club's player of the year and players' player of the year awards.

Sarr went on to score four goals for Senegal at the 2026 World Cup, after featuring in a controversial Africa Cup of Nations final in January.

In March, Senegal's final victory over Morocco was overturned after players left the pitch without the authorisation of the referee.

As Senegal appeal to be reawarded with their title at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), Sarr remains proud that his side "became the African champions on the pitch".

Asked about his chances of winning the African Player of the Year award, he said: "I'm proud of the season I've had, both with Crystal Palace and Senegal. It's been a special year, with important trophies and individual achievements.

"But African football has so many outstanding players, and several of them have also had fantastic seasons.

"I'm thinking particularly of my Senegalese brothers Sadio Mane and Pape Gueye, who also deserve recognition for what they've achieved.

"Of course, winning the award would be an incredible honour. Every African player dreams of that.

"But honestly, what matters most to me is seeing the trophy go to Senegal. I'm incredibly proud of what we accomplished together."

KIGALI – Ten entrepreneurs from eight African countries will converge in Kigali next month for the 2026 Africa’s Business Heroes (ABH) Grand Finale, competing for a share of US$1.5 million in grant funding.

The two-day event, scheduled for December 1–2 at the Kigali Convention Centre, will bring together some of the continent’s most promising business founders, investors and corporate leaders.

The finalists were selected from more than 24,000 applications received from all 54 African countries. They secured their places after pitching their businesses during semi-finals held in Nairobi, Kenya, in August.

The 2026 finalists come from Egypt, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, Benin and Côte d’Ivoire. Their businesses span agriculture, healthcare, manufacturing, technology, industry and education.

Agriculture and healthcare account for 60% of the finalists, while women make up 40% of the group. The average age of the entrepreneurs is 35.

The prize structure awards US$300,000 to the overall winner, US$250,000 to the first runner-up and US$150,000 to the second runner-up. The remaining seven finalists will each receive US$100,000, while another US$100,000 is allocated to global immersion training.

Rwanda has increasingly become an important destination for the continental entrepreneurship competition, having hosted several of its major events in recent years.

Kigali hosted the ABH semi-finals in 2022 before hosting both the semi-finals and Grand Finale in 2023.

The competition returned to Kigali for the 2024 edition’s Grand Finale, which was postponed because of the Marburg outbreak and eventually held on March 14–15, 2025. The 2025 edition’s Grand Finale also took place in Kigali, on December 13, 2025.

Rwanda has also produced entrepreneurs who have made it to the competition’s final 10.

By the end of the 2025 edition, six Rwandan entrepreneurs had reached the Top 10. They include Kevine Kagirimpundu of Uzuri K&Y and Christelle Kwizera of Water Access Rwanda, who finished as the second runner-up in 2019.

Others are Francine Munyaneza of Munyax Eco and Yvette Ishimwe of Iriba Water Group, both recognised in 2021; Albert Munyabugingo of Vuba Vuba Africa, who made the 2023 Top 10; and Mukasahaha Diane of DIKAM Ltd, who reached the final 10 in 2025.

However, Rwanda has no representative among the 2026 finalists.

Established by the Jack Ma Foundation and Alibaba Philanthropy, Africa’s Business Heroes is a continental initiative that identifies and supports entrepreneurs developing businesses with economic and social impact.

Beyond financial awards, participants receive mentorship, business training, international exposure and opportunities to connect with investors and business leaders.

The Kigali programme will also include exhibitions and roadshows at universities and entrepreneurship hubs, a founders’ forum on November 30 and the ABH Summit and Labs on December 1.

Among the expected speakers are Rwanda’s Minister of ICT and Innovation, Paula Ingabire; Rwanda Development Board Deputy CEO Juliana Muganza; MTN Uganda CEO Sylvia Mulinge; and Rwanda Green Fund CEO Teddy Mugabo.

The 2026 Grand Finale judging panel will include Bank of Kigali CEO Diane Karusisi and Paystack co-founder and CEO Shola Akinlade, with a third judge yet to be announced.

The winner will be announced on December 2.

The ten entrepreneurs heading to Kigali represent eight African countries and businesses operating in different sectors.

Abitezweho ibisubizo ni abanyeshuri 22 bahawe impamyabumenyi kuri uyu wa Gatanu, bakaba bari bamaze igihe kingana n’umwaka bahugurirwa mu Kigo cy’imbuto cya RICA, aho baherewe ubumenyi bwihariye n’ubushobozi ngiro mu bijyanye n’ikoranabuhanga ry’imbuto n’ubucuruzi bwazo.

MINAGRI yagaragaje ko ubumenyi bahawe bukenewe cyane mu gihugu, kubera ko u Rwanda rwamaze kugera ku bushobozi bwo kuba imbuto nyinshi zikoreshwa mu gihugu by’umwihariko ku bihingwa by’ingenzi 6 (Priority Crops), zituburirwa mu gihugu zitarinze gutumizwa mu mahanga.

Abanyeshuri barangije bakaba bitezweho kongerera ubushobozi inzego zishinzwe urwego rw’imbuto, bakazanagira uruhare mu iterambere ry’ubuhinzi n’impinduka mu buhinzi bw’u Rwanda.

Umunyamabanga Uhoraho muri Minisiteri y’Ubuhinzi n’Ubworozi, Dr. Olivier Kamana, avuga ko bikwiye ko u Rwanda rugira Abanyarwanda bafite ubumenyi buhagije mu bijyanye no gutubura imbuto, bakabikora neza mu buryo bwujuje ubuzirange.

Ati “Mubyo biga harimo cyane cyane n’ibijyanye n’ubuziranenge bw’imbuto, uburyo zitegurwa neza, zikaba zifite ubuziranenge bwose, zidafite indwara kandi zifite ubushobozi bwo kuba zatanga umusaruro mwinshi igihe zikoreshejwe neza n’abahinzi. Ibi rero bizadufasha gukemura ikibazo dukunze guhura nacyo cy’imbuto zitujuje ubuziranenge, zishaje cyangwa se zirwaye, kuko aba banyeshuri bafite ubumenyi butandukanye kandi bugezweho. Ni iby’agaciro ku gihugu cyacu kuko bazazana impinduka nziza mu bijyanye n’urwego rw’ubuhinzi mu Rwanda.”

Abahawe Impamyabumenyi, bavuga ko baje kuba ibisubizo by’ibibazo bigaragara mu rwego rw’imbuto, kuko ubumenyi bahawe bubaha ubushobozi bwo guhangana nabyo no kubyaza umusaruro amahirwe ari muri urwo rwego.

David Kwihangana, avuga ko amasomo bize azabafasha kuba bakongera ingano y’imbuto iboneka ku isoko ry’u Rwanda bafatanyije n'abakora mu rwego rw’imbuto.

Ati “Ikindi bizadufasha ni uguhanga udushya, ni ukuvuga imbuto iza gusubiza ibibazo by’abahinzi, kuko bagiye bari mu byiciro bitandukanye, mu Turere dutandukanye, ubwo rero bakenera imbuto yihanganira ibihe by’izuba, iyihanganira ibihe by’amapfa aho imvura ari nke. Ndatekereza tuzanye ibisubizo ku isoko.”

Christelle Marie Assumpta Uwarugira, avuga ko bamaze igihe kingana n’umwaka biga ibijyanye n’imbuto kugira ngo bamenya ukuntu bazongerera agaciro mu Rwanda.

Ati “Mbere ntarajya kwiga hari nk’amakosa yajyaga aba mu bijyanye n’ubuziranenge, kandi iyo nta buziranenge buhari n’ubundi ntacyo muba muri gukora, kuko akenshi usanga n’umusaruro waragabanutse. Ariko guhugurwa mu buziranenge byaramfashije kubera ko wa musaruro twiteze na za mbuto zihanganira ibihe tuba turimo tubasha kubibona.”

Umuyobozi Mukuru wa One Acre Fund mu Rwanda, Belinda Bwiza, yavuze ko kubona imbuto nziza ari imwe mu nzira zifasha abahinzi bato kongera umusaruro n’amafaranga binjiza.

Yagize ati “Imbuto nziza niryo shingiro ry’inyungu z’umuhinzi muto. Guhugura abantu bayobora amasosiyete y’imbuto no kuzibyaza umusaruro, ni ugushyiraho urufatiro rurambye rw’amafaranga abahinzi binjiza n’umutekano w’ibiribwa mu Karere.”

Umuyobozi Mukuru wungirje wa RICA, Dr. Momar Dieng, yavuze ko mu byumweru 43, abarangije bahuguwe mu kwita ku bimera, indwara zibasira ibimera no gukora ubucuruzi, banakora ubushakashatsi bushingiye ku gukemura ibibazo biri mu buhinzi.

Yagaragaje ko imishinga bakoze yibanze ku kongera ikoreshwa ry’imbuto z’indobanure, kunoza umusaruro w’imbuto, kubungabunga ubutaka no gukoresha ikoranabuhanga mu kongera umusaruro.

Ikigo cya RICA Seed Center cyatangijwe mu 2022, kiba kimaze guhura abanyeshuri 54 bari mu byiciro bitatu, aho bose bagikora mu rwego rw’ubuhinzi, kuko abarenga 70% bakora mu masosiyete y’imbuto cyangwa bagakora ubushakashatsi bwo ku rwego rwo hejuru, mu gihe abagera 30% batangiye imishinga yabo ijyanye n’imbuto.

Imibare ya Minisiteri y’Ubuhinzi n’ubworozi yo muri uyu mwaka igaragaza ko hafi 50% by'abahinzi mu Rwanda ari bo bakoresha imbuto zifite ubuziranenge, mu gihe ku bahinzi bakora ubuhinzi bunini, ikoreshwa ryazo rirenze 80%.
